items.prose: A market is calm or stressed each week. $P = \begin{pmatrix}0.7 & 0.3\\ 0.1 & 0.9\end{pmatrix}$, rows and columns in the order calm, stressed.
items.question: What is the long-run share of calm weeks?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Balance the flows between the states, then normalise.

byKey.swap: 0.75 is the stressed share. You used $a/(a + b)$.
byKey.diag: 0.7 is the one-week chance calm stays calm.
byKey.half: Stressed weeks are stickier, so they get more of the time.

explain.text: Flow out of calm, $0.3\pi_1$, equals flow in, $0.1\pi_2$. With $\pi_1 + \pi_2 = 1$ this gives $\pi_1 = 0.1/0.4 = 0.25$. Three weeks in four are stressed.

items.prose: A stock's bid-ask spread is 1, 2 or 3 ticks. Each second it moves by the chain $P = \begin{pmatrix}0.7 & 0.3 & 0\\ 0.3 & 0.5 & 0.2\\ 0 & 0.4 & 0.6\end{pmatrix}$, rows and columns in the order 1, 2, 3 ticks.
items.question: What is the long-run average spread, in ticks?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find $\pi$ by elimination, then weight the spreads by it.

byKey.simple: You averaged 1, 2 and 3 equally. The chain spends less time at 3 ticks.
byKey.col: You may have weighted by the middle row of $P$. The weights are the long-run shares $\pi$.

explain.text: Column 1 gives $0.3\pi_1 = 0.3\pi_2$, so $\pi_2 = \pi_1$; column 3 gives $0.4\pi_3 = 0.2\pi_2$, so $\pi_3 = \tfrac12\pi_1$. Normalising, $\pi = (0.4, 0.4, 0.2)$. The average spread is $0.4 + 0.8 + 0.6 = 1.8$ ticks.

items.question: Select all that apply: which converge to one $\pi$ from every start?

options.why: The swap is irreducible but has period 2, so $P^k$ alternates.
Each state is its own closed class. The chain stays wherever it starts.

feedback.correct: Irreducible with a self-loop somewhere: all three converge.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check each chain for irreducible and aperiodic.

byKey.swap: The swap is irreducible but has period 2, so $P^k$ alternates.
byKey.id: Each state is its own closed class. The chain stays wherever it starts.

explain.text: The first three are irreducible, and each has a self-loop, which rules out a period. The third reaches $\pi = (\tfrac13, \tfrac23)$ although state 1 never stays put. The swap is periodic and the identity is reducible.

items.prose: States 1 and 2 form a closed class, and state 3 is absorbing. From state 4 the chain stays with chance 0.5, moves to 1 with 0.2, or moves to 3 with 0.3.
items.question: Starting at 4, what is the long-run chance the chain is in the class $\{1, 2\}$?

widget.label: Chance of ending in the class 1, 2

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Treat entering the class as absorption and use first-step analysis from 4.

byKey.step: 0.2 is the one-step chance. The chain can wait at 4 and try again.
byKey.unique: You split evenly between the two places to end. The chances 0.2 and 0.3 are not equal.
byKey.other: 0.6 is the chance of ending at 3.

explain.text: Once the chain enters $\{1, 2\}$ or reaches 3 it never leaves, so both act as absorbing. First-step analysis from 4 gives $h = 0.5h + 0.2$, so $h = 0.4$. The limit depends on the start because the chain is reducible.

items.prose: A fair walk on 0 to 5 is absorbed at 0 and 5. It starts at 2.
items.question: What is the expected number of steps to absorption?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write $t_i = 1 + \tfrac12 t_{i-1} + \tfrac12 t_{i+1}$ for $i = 1$ to 4, with $t_0 = t_5 = 0$.

byKey.dist: 2 is the distance to the nearest end. The walk wanders, so it takes longer.
byKey.four: 4 is $t_1$, from the start next to 0.
byKey.nine: You may have squared the distance to the far end. The pattern is $i(5 - i)$.

explain.text: By symmetry $t_1 = t_4$ and $t_2 = t_3$. Then $t_1 = 1 + \tfrac12 t_2$ and $t_2 = 1 + \tfrac12 t_1 + \tfrac12 t_2$ give $t_1 = 4$ and $t_2 = 6$. That fits $t_i = i(5 - i)$.

items.prose: A loan is rated A or B each year until it is repaid or defaults. From A: stay 0.3, to B 0.1, repaid 0.5, default 0.1. From B: to A 0.2, stay 0.4, repaid 0.2, default 0.2.
items.question: What is the expected remaining life of a B loan, in years?

widget.label: Expected life of a B loan

byKey.geo: You used $1/(1 - 0.4)$, as if B could only stay or end. B loans can move up to A first.
byKey.a: 1.75 years is the life of an A loan.
byKey.drop: You dropped the $+1$. Each year passes before the loan moves.

explain.text: The equations are $0.7t_A - 0.1t_B = 1$ and $-0.2t_A + 0.6t_B = 1$. Eliminating gives $t_A = 1.75$ and $t_B = 2.25$. Equivalently, the rows of $(I - Q)^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix}1.5 & 0.25\\ 0.5 & 1.75\end{pmatrix}$ add to $t$.

items.prose: Each year a loan is repaid with chance 0.2, defaults with chance 0.05, and otherwise carries on unchanged.
items.question: What is the chance it is eventually repaid?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Condition on the first year: $h = 0.75h + 0.2 \times 1 + 0.05 \times 0$.

byKey.year: 0.2 is the chance of repayment in the first year. The loan gets more years.
byKey.carry: 0.75 is the chance the loan carries on for a year.

explain.text: First-step analysis: $h = 0.75h + 0.2$, so $h = 0.2/0.25 = 0.8$. Of the years in which the loan ends, 0.2 in 0.25 are repayments. Default takes the other 20%.

items.prose: A walk on 0 to 3 is absorbed at 0 and 3. From 1 or 2 it steps up with chance $\tfrac13$ and down with chance $\tfrac23$. It starts at 2.
items.question: What is the chance it reaches 3 before 0?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Solve $h_1 = \tfrac13 h_2$ and $h_2 = \tfrac23 h_1 + \tfrac13$.

byKey.fair: $\tfrac23$ is the fair walk's answer. The drift is downwards here.
byKey.step: $\tfrac13$ is the chance of stepping straight to 3. The walk can also come back to 2 later.
byKey.up: $\tfrac67$ is the answer for an upward drift. Here up has chance $\tfrac13$.
byKey.h1: $\tfrac17$ is $h_1$, from the start next to 0.

explain.text: Substitute $h_1 = \tfrac13 h_2$: $h_2 = \tfrac29 h_2 + \tfrac13$, so $\tfrac79 h_2 = \tfrac13$ and $h_2 = \tfrac37$. Then $h_1 = \tfrac17$. The downward drift pulls both well below the fair values.
